Three things you should know about fog nets

A primer on a quiet and frankly odd piece of water engineering.

By
  • Ada Rivers
October 22, 2026

How much do you know about fog nets?

Maybe, like me, you have seen a photo of one strung across a hillside, that it catches water from the air … and that is about the extent of it.

The good news for both of us is that my colleague Bo Lindqvist just published two long stories about fog nets. His reporting took him to a dry stretch of coast, where he climbed a ridge before dawn to watch the nets drip, and to learn how this odd material could change the water supply of whole villages.

I would recommend you give both of his stories a read. There is one feature about the people who mend the nets every season, as well as a look at how engineers are trying to make the mesh catch more water. Here are three things I took away.

Fog nets are a large and quiet water source

A fog net is a sheet of fine mesh stretched between two poles, facing the wind. Fog drifts through it, tiny droplets stick to the threads, merge, grow heavy, and run down into a gutter at the bottom.

That means a single net can collect a surprising amount of water on a good morning, without pumps, power or moving parts. But the yield swings wildly from one day to the next, and a dry week can leave a village waiting.

The steady change in coastal weather has already shifted where the thickest fog settles, and some ridges that were reliable a decade ago now see far fewer foggy mornings, which leaves their nets hanging dry.

The odd thing is, only a few of the planning models used by water agencies account for fog at all, and none of them track how quickly the fog belts are moving, or which villages will lose them first.

Wind can make or break a net

Wind is what carries fog into the mesh in the first place, so a calm morning yields almost nothing. Too much wind, though, can tear the mesh, bend the poles, or blow the droplets straight through before they can gather.

Today, the practice in most villages is to take the nets down before storms, which costs a day of work each time, and means a missed harvest whenever the forecast is wrong.

Engineers at a small coastal institute are building a mesh with a coating that sheds water faster, so that more droplets reach the gutter before the wind takes them.

That is only the start, since once the mesh works, the nets need sturdier frames, better gutters, and a way to store the water for dry days.

The economics of fog nets are surprisingly complicated

A good net costs little to build, but the frames, tanks and repairs add up, and the yield depends on weather that nobody controls.

One particularly big wrinkle: the same fog that feeds the nets also feeds the plants on the ridge, and taking too much of it may dry them out.

Researchers are working to better understand how much water a ridge can give up, and how that changes from one season to the next.

The more nets we put up, the more we will need to know about them.
